Perception, family, distance · 2000

Yi YiThe Lives We Miss When We Look Too Quickly

Marina’s Dreams reviews Edward Yang’s Yi Yi, a precise and tender Taipei family drama about perception, distance, and the lives hidden in plain sight.

By MarinaOctober 17, 20263 min readSpoiler-light review

In this review

Seeing Beyond the FrameThe Cost of Looking CarefullySources & references
Film
Yi Yi
Director
Edward Yang
Year
2000

Edward Yang’s Yi Yi looks at a Taipei family without turning its members into lessons. Over roughly a year, a wedding, a child’s school life, a father’s work, and a family crisis gather into one spacious domestic rhythm. The film’s title suggests a pair, and Yang keeps returning to doubled perspectives: what one person feels, what another can see, and the distance between them. I love how ordinary the circumstances remain while the emotional weather keeps changing. Its scale is expansive, but its attention stays close to faces, gestures, and the quiet negotiations of daily life.

Seeing Beyond the Frame

The film’s most distinctive idea arrives through Yang-Yang, the young son who photographs the backs of people’s heads. His camera is not a cute plot device; it gives visual form to the family’s blind spots. Yang’s compositions do something similar. Windows, doorways, mirrors, and reflections divide the frame, letting one conversation continue beside another. Taipei is not mere background either: offices, apartments, elevators, and neon streets press gently on the characters, shaping choices they think are private.

That precision never makes the people feel diagrammed. Wu Nien-jen plays NJ with a wonderfully contained uncertainty, a man whose politeness cannot quite conceal his longing. Elaine Jin gives Min-Min a fragile, inward gravity, while the younger performers make awkwardness feel unperformed rather than cute. Issey Ogata’s Mr. Ota brings a different register, speaking about music and life with an openness that briefly loosens the family’s guarded language. The ensemble makes small hesitations feel consequential.

I also admire the film’s soundscape: office hum, traffic, keyboards, footsteps, and music occupy the same moral world as the dialogue. Silence is not emptiness here; it is often the residue of things people cannot say without changing the room. Yang allows scenes to run past their obvious endpoint, then finds a new emotional angle in the extra beat. The result is a rare feeling of lived time, as if the film is listening for meaning rather than announcing it. Even recurring sounds seem to remember what the characters have tried to leave behind, giving the city a soft but persistent pulse.

The Cost of Looking Carefully

Still, Yi Yi asks for patience, and its generosity can become a limitation. The long running time and many parallel threads sometimes soften the pressure of individual scenes; a few relationships feel more observed than fully opened. The film’s balance can also keep sharper conflict at arm’s length. Yet that reserve is partly its argument. Families do not offer clean arcs, and a person’s most important change may be invisible to everyone nearby—including the person changing.

What stays with me is the film’s belief that attention is an ethical act. To look carefully does not solve anyone’s problems, but it can make another life less mysterious and less easy to dismiss. Yi Yi finds scale in the everyday: a child’s question, a work decision, a face glimpsed through glass. Its beauty is not polished distance; it is the patient shock of discovering how much reality exists just outside our angle of view.
